items.question_text: Your application is running on Google Cloud in a managed instance group (MIG). You see errors in Cloud Logging for one VM that one of the processes is not responsive. You want to replace this VM in the MIG quickly. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
The `gcloud compute instance-groups managed recreate-instances` command allows you to delete and immediately recreate specific instances within a Managed Instance Group based on the current instance template.
This is the most direct and efficient method to replace a single unresponsive VM without updating the group's template or performing manual console actions.

choices.text: Use the gcloud compute instances update command with a REFRESH action for the VM.
Use the gcloud compute instance-groups managed recreate-instances command to recreate the VM.
Select the MIG from the Compute Engine console and, in the menu, select Replace VMs.
Update and apply the instance template of the MIG.

items.question_text: You want to permanently delete a Pub/Sub topic managed by Config Connector in your Google Cloud project. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Google Cloud Config Connector is a Kubernetes-native service that allows users to manage GCP resources using standard Kubernetes tools and APIs.
To delete a resource managed by Config Connector, such as a Pub/Sub topic, you must use `kubectl` to remove the corresponding custom resource from the cluster. The Config Connector controller detects this deletion and propagates the request to the Google Cloud API to permanently delete the underlying infrastructure resource.

choices.text: Use kubectl to create the label deleted-by-cnrm and to change its value to true for the topic resource.
Use kubectl to delete the topic resource.
Use gcloud CLI to delete the topic.
Use gcloud CLI to update the topic label managed-by-cnrm to false.

items.question_text: Your company is using Google Workspace to manage employee accounts. Anticipated growth will increase the number of personnel from 100 employees to 1,000 employees within 2 years. Most employees will need access to your company’s Google Cloud account. The systems and processes will need to support 10x growth without performance degradation, unnecessary complexity, or security issues. What should you do?
items.solution_text: Option B is correct because organizing users into groups enables scalable access management via Cloud IAM, avoiding the complexity of assigning permissions to thousands of individual users. Enforcing multi-factor authentication addresses security requirements without introducing unnecessary architectural changes. Options A and D introduce redundant or external identity providers, while Option C suggests a non-existent federation feature between Workspace and Cloud Identity.

choices.text: Migrate the users to Active Directory. Connect the Human Resources system to Active Directory. Turn on Google Cloud Directory Sync (GCDS) for Cloud Identity. Turn on Identity Federation from Cloud Identity to Active Directory.
Organize the users in Cloud Identity into groups. Enforce multi-factor authentication in Cloud Identity.
Turn on identity federation between Cloud Identity and Google Workspace. Enforce multi-factor authentication for domain wide delegation.
Use a third-party identity provider service through federation. Synchronize the users from Google Workplace to the third-party provider in real time.

items.question_text: You want to host your video encoding software on Compute Engine. Your user base is growing rapidly, and users need to be able to encode their videos at any time without interruption or CPU limitations. You must ensure that your encoding solution is highly available, and you want to follow Google-recommended practices to automate operations. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Option D is correct because Managed Instance Groups (MIGs) are the recommended Google Cloud architecture for stateless workloads requiring high availability and automated scaling.
Configuring autoscaling based on CPU utilization directly addresses the requirement to handle rapid growth and avoid CPU limitations by automatically adding instances when demand spikes.
Unlike options A and B, MIGs provide built-in health checks and distribution across zones, while option C suggests manual intervention rather than the requested automation.

choices.text: Deploy your solution on multiple standalone Compute Engine instances, and increase the number of existing instances when CPU utilization on Cloud Monitoring reaches a certain threshold.
Deploy your solution on multiple standalone Compute Engine instances, and replace existing instances with high-CPU instances when CPU utilization on Cloud Monitoring reaches a certain threshold.
Deploy your solution to an instance group, and increase the number of available instances whenever you see high CPU utilization in Cloud Monitoring.
Deploy your solution to an instance group, and set the autoscaling based on CPU utilization.

items.question_text: Your managed instance group raised an alert stating that new instance creation has failed to create new instances. You need to solve the instance creation problem. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Instance templates in Google Cloud are immutable, meaning they cannot be modified after creation. If a managed instance group fails to create instances due to template issues, you must verify the syntax and potentially create a new valid template rather than editing the existing one.

Additionally, persistent disk names within a project must be unique; if previous failed attempts created disks with the same name as the intended instances, these conflicting resources must be deleted before new instances can be successfully provisioned.

choices.text: Create an instance template that contains valid syntax which will be used by the instance group. Delete any persistent disks with the same name as instance names.
Create an instance template that contains valid syntax that will be used by the instance group. Verify that the instance name and persistent disk name values are not the same in the template.

Verify that the instance template being used by the instance group contains valid syntax. Delete any persistent disks with the same name as instance names. Set the disks.autoDelete property to true in the instance template.

Delete the current instance template and replace it with a new instance template. Verify that the instance name and persistent disk name values are not the same in the template. Set the disks.autoDelete property to true in the instance template.
